passages.text: Reminder : “singular” forms are the je , tu , and il/elle forms because those are the singular subjects; “plural” forms are the nous , vous , and ils/elles forms, because those are the plural subjects. See section B.2 from chapter 1 if you need to review this.
passages.section_title: B.2 Regular verbs in the present tense

passages.text: The “stem” ( la racine ) plus the “ending” ( la terminaison ) form the complete verb form. If we take the infinitive finir , “fin” is the stem and “ir” is the infinitive ending. In the form nous répondons , “répond” is the stem and “ons” is the ending.
passages.section_title: B.2 Regular verbs in the present tense

passages.text: The endings ( terminaisons ) for regular verbs are the same for every verb in that group. You must memorize these endings.
passages.section_title: B.2 Regular verbs in the present tense

passages.text: The -ent ending on the ils/elles form is silent. This is especially important for -er verbs, as it means four of the six forms ( je, tu, il, and ils ) are pronounced exactly the same, although they are written differently. This is why the subject noun or pronoun must be used in French; if you only said the verb form (as occurs in Spanish, for example), people would not know who you were talking about.
passages.section_title: B.2 Regular verbs in the present tense

passages.text: The plural forms of the -ir verbs all have -iss-, but the singular forms do not.
passages.section_title: B.2 Regular verbs in the present tense

passages.text: You hear the “d” sound in the plural forms of the -re verbs, but not in the singular forms.
passages.section_title: B.2 Regular verbs in the present tense

passages.text: For your information, about 95% of French verbs are -er verbs. All -er verbs with the exception of aller (to go) are regular, except for minor spelling-related changes that occur within the stem. The endings for all -er verbs (except aller ) are the same.
passages.section_title: B.2 Regular verbs in the present tense

passages.text: Since all -er verbs are regular (except for some spelling changes in the stem), this means that irregular verbs fall into the -ir and -re categories. When you want to conjugate a new -ir or -re verb, therefore, you need to find out if it is regular or irregular.

je forms: -er verbs end in -e, other verbs end in -s | This is true for almost all verbs. The only exceptions in the present tense are j’ai and je peux (I can)/ je veux (I want). Apart from these, the ending for je forms will always be -e or -s.

passages.text: We generally refer to this tense as the “present,” but its full name is the “present indicative.” The present tense in French corresponds to three different forms in English: the simple present, the emphatic present, and the present progressive. In other words, je mange means “I eat,” “I do eat,” and “I am eating.” Students sometimes get confused when trying to translate the English in their heads into French, and will try to combine two verbs ( être and manger ) to come up with the French for “I am eating.” However, that would make no sense in French – you just say je mange . Similarly, we have already seen that in English, “do” is used as a question marker; to ask “Do you speak French,” we just ask a question in French using the present tense of parler , plus either est-ce que or inversion, as described in chapter 1: Est-ce que vous parlez français? or Parlez-vous français? It is important to remember that French is not a weird form of English – the two languages do not correspond word-for-word and you need to try as hard as you can to incorporate French speech patterns from the beginning of your study, and not just concentrate on learning specific words.

Don’t worry! You do not need to memorize all this information now. However, seeing it as you begin your study of French verbs is useful for many students. If you can absorb the basic idea that all tu forms end in -s, for example, and that il forms never do, that will save you from many mistakes!

In this chapter you will be asked only to memorize the conjugation for -er verbs. The -er group is by far the most common, comprising almost 95% of French verbs. Before we move on, let’s practice this -er conjugation a few times. The other regular groups (-ir and -re) will be reviewed in subsequent chapters, and you do not need to practice or learn them now.

An excellent way to practice verb endings on your own is simply to choose a regular verb and write it out several times as you do in this exercise. You can always check your answers at an online conjugator such as http://leconjugueur.lefigaro.fr/.

Flashcards for vocabulary and verb forms are also very helpful for many people, but looking at material is never as effective a study method as producing it yourself, so use flashcards to supplement your written practice, not replace it. You might try color-coding the endings on your flashcards if you are more visually oriented.

There are many websites where you can practice verbs online, for example the ex cellent U Texas Austin site, http://laits.utexas.edu/fi/vp/, and apps available for smart phones. Try out various options to see what best suits your learning style.

Two important irregular verbs to be aware of are vouloir (to want) and devoir (to have to, must). These verbs will be memorized in chapter 5; however, you can begin to recognize their forms now: je veux (I want), tu veux, il veut, nous voulons, vous voulez, ils veulent je dois (I must), tu dois, il doit, nous devons, vous devez, ils doivent The conditional forms j e voudrais (I would like) and je devrais (I should) are also very common.

Very often, you will need to use two verbs together. If the verbs function together and belong to the same subject, you only conjugate one of them; the second one remains in the infinitive. This is just like English.

passages.text: In chapter 1 ( B.8 ), you were introduced to the three main ways to ask questions in French: intonation, inversion, and est-ce que . In this chapter, we would like you to begin using est-ce que and inversion to ask questions in French. Right now, you will focus on yes/no questions; that is, questions which will be answered by a “yes” or “no” answer. You will also understand and be able to answer questions requiring more information (who, why, what, etc.), and you will gradually become more familiar with them; in chapter 6, you will practice forming informational questions yourself.

To ask a question with est-ce que, you simply place Est-ce que in front of the subject of a declarative sentence. It does not matter whether the subject is a noun or a pronoun. Remember that est-ce que has no real meaning in the sentence; it simply signals that you are about to ask a question, just as the word do usually signals that a question is coming in English (e.g. Do you speak French? ). Est-ce que is pronounced [ε skə] – the “s” sound is from the ce , since the letters “st” in the verb est are silent. If the word immediately following “est-ce que” begins with a vowel or a silent h, you will change que to qu’ . Remember that this is called élision . Observe the following examples.

Phrase déclarative | Question

Hélène aime le café. (Helen likes coffee.) | Est-ce qu’Hélène aime le café? (Does Helen like coffee?)
Les professeurs sont stricts. (The teachers are strict.) | Est-ce que les professeurs sont stricts? (Are the teachers strict?)

This “t” is added when the verb ends in a written vowel and the subject pronoun also begins with a vowel, to avoid having two vowels together. Since most verb forms end in a consonant, this can occur only with third person singular forms ( il, elle, on ) of -er verbs and the verbs avoir ( il a ) and aller ( il va ), where the verb forms end in a vowel. passages.text: Inversion is used less often in spoken French than either intonation or est-ce que . However, it is the form you will see most often in written French. Additionally, inversion is not used when the subject is “je. ”

Since inversion is done between the subject pronoun and the verb, you must have a subject pronoun in order to do inversion. If the subject is a noun instead of a pronoun, the only way to do inversion is to reduplicate the noun with the appropriate pronoun . If the noun is a masculine singular noun, for example, the appropriate pronoun would be “il.” You keep the noun in the usual position (before the verb), but you also invert the verb and the added pronoun. French has several different constructions that correspond to the English interrogative what . In this chapter, we will learn the interrogative adjective quel , which is always used with a noun. Quel can be translated into English as what or as which depending on the context, and even as who if it is referring to a person. Anytime you are asking “What/ which something,” you will use a form of quel in French. Since it is an adjective, quel has four forms. They are all pronounced the same ([kεl]), unless the plural form ( quels , quelles ) makes liaison with a following vowel.

All -er verbs are regular, except the verb aller which you will learn in chapter 4. However, some -er verbs have minor spelling changes. All these changes are for reasons of pronunciation, so if you understand the reason for them, you will find it easy to remember when the spelling change is necessary. Because these changes occur simply in order to maintain the correct pronunciation, these are not true “irregular” verbs like the verbs être and avoir that you have already learned.

The first change occurs in verbs that end in -cer and -ger. Because the letters c and g each have two pronunciations, a spelling change must occur to keep the same pronunciation of the consonant in all six forms. As you remember, the letter c is hard ([k]) before a, o, and u, and soft ([s]) before e and i. The letter g is also hard ([g]) before a, o, and u, and soft ([ ʒ ]) before e and i. Since all -er endings except for the nous form end in -e, we must make a spelling change to the nous form to ensure a soft consonant before the -ons ending. For -ger verbs, we simply add an -e before the -ons. For -cer verbs, we change the -c to -ç, which is always pronounced [s]. All -cer and -ger verbs make these changes in the nous form of the present tense. The other five forms are the same as any other -er verb.

1. Verbs ending in -cer and -ger – Change in the nous form
préf érer ([pre fe re]
je préfère [ʒə pre fεr] | nous préférons [nu pre fe rɔ̃ ]
tu préfères [ty pre fεr] | vous préférez [vu pre fe re]
il/elle préfère [il pre fεr] | ils/elles préfèrent [il pre fεr]
passages.section_title: 1. Verbs ending in -cer and -ger – Change in the nous form
context: 2. Verbs ending in – éCer and -eCer – Change je , tu, il, and ils forms
Image 202

The second type of spelling change occurs in four forms, the je, tu, il, and ils forms. Since these forms visually look like a shoe or a boot when written in the traditional conjugation pattern, many refer to this as the “shoe” or “boot” pattern.

passages.text:
1. Verbs ending in -cer and -ger – Change in the nous form
p eser ([pə ze]
je pèse [ʒə pεz] | nous pesons [nu pə ʒɔ̃ ]
tu pèses [ty pεz] | vous pesez [vu pə ze]
il/elle pèse [il pεz] | ils/elles pèsent [il pεz]
passages.section_title: 1. Verbs ending in -cer and -ger – Change in the nous form

passages.text:
1. Verbs ending in -cer and -ger – Change in the nous form
app eler ([ap le] ou [a pə le])
j’appelle [ʒə pεl] | nous appelons [nu zap lɔ̃ ] ou [nu za pə lɔ̃ ]
tu appelles [ty a pεl] | vous appelez [vu za ple] ou [vu za pə le]
il/elle appelle [i la pεl] | ils/elles appellent [il za pεl]
passages.section_title: 1. Verbs ending in -cer and -ger – Change in the nous form

passages.text: These changes affect all verbs with infinitives ending in -éCer or -eCer, where C represents a single consonant. As you recall from chapter two, the letter “e” has three pronunciations in French: [ ə ], [ ε ], and [e]. French pronunciation rules say that [ ə ] and [e] occur only in open syllables, that is, syllables that end with a vowel sound. In a closed syllable, that is, one ending with a consonant sound, we need the sound [ ε ].
passages.section_title: 1. Verbs ending in -cer and -ger – Change in the nous form

passages.text: Since the je, tu, il, and ils forms of -er verbs are all pronounced the same, with silent verb endings ( -e, -es, -e, -ent ), the last sound in each of these forms is the last consonant of the stem. These four forms must change spelling to match their pronunciation. It is only the stem of the verb, that is, the part before the endings, that changes, so these are known as stem-changing verbs. The endings are still regular -er verb endings.
passages.section_title: 1. Verbs ending in -cer and -ger – Change in the nous form

passages.text: The je, tu, il, and ils forms are all pronounced the same, and contain the accent change from é to è, which changes the vowel sound from [e] to [E]. The nous and vous forms keep the same vowel as the infinitive, written é and pronounced [e]. Note that this change affects only the final accented é in the stem of the verb. As you can see from the example of préférer above, it is the second e that changes (the stem is préfér-), not the first one.
passages.section_title: 2.a. Verbs ending in – éCer, like préférer above

passages.text: The je, tu, il, and ils forms are all pronounced the same, and contain the vowel change from the sound [ ə ] to the sound [ ε ]. The infinitive and the nous and vous forms remain unchanged, with the vowel sound [ ə ].
passages.section_title: 2.b. Verbs ending in -eCer, like peser or appeler above

passages.text: There are two ways for spelling to indicate this pronunciation change. Most verbs in this pattern add an accent grave (è), but a few double the final consonant after the e. Common verbs that add an accent like peser include lever (to raise), enlever (to take off), emmener (to bring) and amener (to take).
passages.section_title: 2.b. Verbs ending in -eCer, like peser or appeler above

passages.text: Since the spelling reform of 1990, the only remaining verbs that double the consonant are the verbs appeler and jeter ( to throw ) and their families (e.g. épeler (to spell ), rejeter (to reject )).
passages.section_title: 2.b. Verbs ending in -eCer, like peser or appeler above

passages.text:
3. Verbs ending in -ayer, -oyer, -uyer
bal ayer ([ba la je]
je balaie [ʒə ba lε] | nous balayons [nu ba lε jɔ̃ ]
tu balaies [ty ba lε] | vous balayez [vu ba lε je]
il/elle balaie [il ba lε] | ils/elles balaient [il ba lε]

3. Verbs ending in -ayer, -oyer, -uyer
nett oyer ([nə twa je]
je nettoie [ʒə nε twa] | nous nettoyons [nu nε twa jɔ̃ ]
tu nettoies [ty nε twa] | vous nettoyez [vu nε twa je]
il/elle nettoie [il nε twa] | ils/elles nettoient [il nε twa]

3. Verbs ending in -ayer, -oyer, -uyer
ess uyer ([ε sɥi je]
j’essuie [ʒə sɥi] | nous essuyons [nu zε sɥi jɔ̃]
tu essuies [ty ε sɥi] | vous essuyez [vu zε sɥi je]
il/elle essuie [i lε sɥi] | ils/elles essuient [il zε sɥi]

In these forms, the -y- changes to -i- in the je, tu, il , and ils forms, but remains unchanged in the nous and vous forms. (With verbs of the -ayer type, you have the choice of changing or not changing, but since the change is required in the other two types (-oyer and -uyer), it is easiest just to learn that all three of these types change in the shoe pattern.)
For practice, consult the charts above and write the correct form of the verb in the present tense.
Je (préférer) ___________ la salsa.
Mon cours de français (commencer) ___________à 10h50.
Il s’(appeler) ___________ Georges.
Nous (nettoyer) ___________la cuisine tous les jours.
Mon frère (essuyer) ___________la vaisselle.
Nous (ranger) ___________nos affaires sur les étagères.
Mes amis (balayer) ___________leur chambre.
Jean n’(essayer) ___________pas de nouvelles choses.
Nous (commencer) ___________à parler français!
Mon sac à dos (peser) ___________lourd.
À quelle heure (emmener) ___________-vous votre fille à l’école?
Qu’est-ce que vous (manger) ___________?
Vous (préférer) ___________les oranges ou les pommes?
Les clients (payer) ___________à la caisse.

*Note: There are three set phrases that invert with “je”: suis-je? ai-je? and puis-je? (the latter (“may I?”) is an obsolete form of “je peux,” used only in this context). Since one doesn’t really ask questions about oneself very often, this is not something you need to remember in first-year French.

* Note: If the question contains an interrogative word and is very short, basically just the subject and verb, one occasionally sees the noun inverted; for example, “Où est le train?” Do not worry if you see this structure!

The first chapter focuses on the greetings and farewells of French Canadians. We will explore “la bise” and the use of “tu” and “vous”. We will examine the song “Bonjour mon ami” by Angèle Arsenault. This chapter will also highlight the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the traditional greeting of “la bise”.
French-Canadian ways to say “Hello” and “Goodbye”

In French-speaking Canada, “bonjour” can be a greeting and a farewell; it can be used to say both “hello” and “goodbye.” Furthermore, the expressions “bon matin” and “bon après-midi” are greetings used in Canada to say, “good morning” and “good afternoon”, respectively. “Bon matin” and “bon après-midi” are not commonly heard in French-speaking European countries. For instance, in France, they do not say “bon matin.” To say, “good morning” in France, you simply say “bonjour.” “Bon après-midi” is used in France however, only when someone is leaving, not as a greeting.
Questions de réflexion
Think about how you usually say hello or goodbye to people. Does the way you interact with people change depending on the person or the setting? How? Give examples.
Does technology impact your greetings or farewells? How? Give examples.

In French Canada, just like in other French-speaking countries, when people say hello, goodbye and congratulations to their friends and family, they will lightly kiss each other on the cheek (se faire la bise); however, worldwide, different countries “font la bise” differently. In Canada, you kiss each cheek once for a total of two kisses, but in Europe, this number can vary. For example, they kiss three times in parts of Belgium, the Netherlands and Switzerland. Furthermore, there may be one to four kisses in different regions of France. Just like the number of kisses can vary, where these kisses start can, too; in Canada and Paris, we always start “la bise” on the left and finish on the right. If you are interested in seeing a visual of the number of kisses shared per location, click the following link ; you will be taken to a colour-coded map of the number of kisses given in different French-speaking regions of Europe.

passages.text: When you meet someone new, do you shake hands or make any other kind of physical contact? What about when you greet someone you know? What about family or coworkers?

passages.section_title: How to “faire la bise” in French Canada!

passages.text: The pronouns “tu” and “vous” both mean “you.” Generally speaking, “tu” is the singular form used when speaking to family members, friends or peers, and “vous” is used in both the singular form when talking to older people, authority figures and strangers and the plural form used when speaking to a group. This dichotomy is common in many French-speaking regions; however, French-speaking Canadiens use “tu” much more often. For example, Canadians may use “tu” to speak to a cashier they do not know. When in doubt, to be respectful, start with “vous.” You can always switch to “tu” if the person you are speaking with tells you it is okay to do so.
Questions de réflexion

In the English language, we do not make the distinction between the second-person formal and informal as we do in French with “tu” and “vous.” How do you show respect when speaking to a stranger or authority figure in English?
Think about when you meet someone new. Is there a certain way that you like to be spoken to by strangers?

Le deuxième chapitre s’intéresse aux différents dialectes et aux variations de vocabulaire entre le français parlé au Canada et celui parlé en France. Nous analyserons la chanson « J’aime ta grand-mère » par Les Trois Accords. De plus, nous examinerons le français parlé en Côte d’Ivoire, en particulier l’usage du Nouchi. Ce chapitre mettra en lumière les variations linguistiques et la manière dont elles façonnent l’identité culturelle de chaque région.

Dans ce chapitre, nous avons appris le vocabulaire de la salle de classe et de la famille. Au Canada francophone, nous avons développé nos propres dialectes. Le français est parlé par 22,8 % de la population canadienne. 85,4 % des francophones du Canada vivent au Québec. Près de 10,4 millions de Canadiens peuvent avoir une conversation en français. Nous utilisons, au Canada, de nombreux mots de vocabulaire qui n’existent pas dans les autres régions francophones du monde. Par exemple, au Canada, « une copine » est souvent appelée « une blonde » (“girlfriend”). De plus, « une gomme » s’appelle « une efface » (“eraser”) au Canada. Enfin, au Canada, on dit « bienvenue » pour signifier la même chose que « de rien » (“you’re welcome”). Avec plus de 10 millions de personnes qui parlent français au Canada, il est logique que la langue évolue.

Pouvez-vous penser à des mots anglais que nous utilisons au Canada mais que les étrangers d’autres pays anglophones n’utilisent pas ? Lesquels ?

Le troisième chapitre couvre les horaires, le temps libre et les carrières. Dans ce chapitre, nous allons examiner les différences entre les heures de travail au Canada et en France. Nous allons aussi écouter une chanson de la chanteuse canadienne Lisa Leblanc qui fait des blagues sur la façon dont elle passe son temps. Finalement, nous allons explorer la semaine française à la Nouvelle-Orléans.

En France, la loi exige que les personnes ne travaillent pas plus de 11 heures consécutives. C’est pourquoi la journée de travail commence généralement après 8 h 30. Cependant, la plupart des travailleurs se rendent au travail entre 9 h et 9 h 45. En France, il y a généralement une pause-café vers 10 h 30. Le déjeuner se déroule de 12 h à 14 h. Il y a une autre pause-café vers 15 h 30. Les travailleurs ne partent généralement pas avant 18 h 30 à 19 h. Au Canada, les heures de travail normales sont du lundi au vendredi, entre 8 h (ou 8 h 30) et 17 h. Les travailleurs ont droit à une pause dîner non payée de 30 minutes pour chaque période de cinq heures de travail. Si le travailleur doit rester disponible pour travailler pendant sa pause, l’employeur doit lui offrir des pauses repas payées. Normalement, la semaine de travail comprend entre 35 et 40 heures. Les travailleurs ont également droit à deux jours de repos par semaine. Généralement, c’est samedi et dimanche.

passages.text: La Louisiane est sans doute l’État le plus « français » des États-Unis. Ancienne colonie française, elle a été marquée par une forte influence culturelle et linguistique française. La Louisiane est le lieu où les gens parlent diverses langues, telles que le français, l’acadien, l’anglais, le créole et l’espagnol. En conséquence, cette région est souvent décrite comme un véritable « melting pot » de cultures et de langues. Cependant, pendant longtemps, le français a été marginalisé en Louisiane, et de nombreux politiciens ont contribué à l’assimilation de la population francophone à la culture américaine dominante. Ceci a conduit à une forte baisse de l’utilisation de la langue française dans la communauté francophone. Toutefois, en 1968, la situation a commencé à changer avec la création du CODOFIL (Council for the Development of French in Louisiana). Le CODOFIL a lutté et continue de lutter pour la préservation et la promotion du français et de la culture francophone en Louisiane. Grâce à ces efforts, le français a retrouvé une place plus importante dans la société louisianaise. C’est un changement majeur dans l’histoire linguistique de l’État. Découvrez comment les musiciens, artistes, journalistes et boulangers contribuent à la promotion de la culture française à la Nouvelle-Orléans en regardant cette vidéo.

C’est le bon moment pour signaler que nous utilisons des noms différents pour nos repas au Canada et en France. Au Canada, le petit-déjeuner est le déjeuner, le déjeuner est le dîner et le dîner est le souper.
